subject_title: Accessibility, Usability, Compatibility, and Internationalization Assurance
theoretical_foundations:
Accessibility assurance is a socio-technical quality problem, not a scanner-score problem. The normative baseline for web content is WCAG 2.2, published as ISO/IEC 40500:2025 and as a W3C Recommendation. WCAG is organized around Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, and Robust principles; conformance is claimable only when every applicable success criterion at the selected level is satisfied for the full page or complete process, or a conforming alternate version is supplied. WCAG 2.2 added criteria especially relevant to cognition, low vision, and mobile use, including Focus Not Obscured, Dragging Movements, Target Size (Minimum), Consistent Help, Redundant Entry, and Accessible Authentication. Its criteria are normative and testable, but examples and techniques are informative. WCAG explicitly acknowledges that it cannot cover every type, degree, or combination of disability, so conformance is necessary evidence rather than proof of universal usability.

The principal engineering abstraction is the accessibility tree: semantic names, roles, states, properties, relationships, focus order, and status changes must survive the browser/operating-system accessibility API boundary to assistive technology. Prefer native HTML/platform controls; use ARIA to supply missing semantics and keep dynamic state synchronized. A visually convincing custom widget can still be absent, mislabeled, unfocusable, or incorrectly announced. Keyboard and switch-equivalent operation, visible and non-obscured focus, logical reading order, non-color cues, text alternatives, captions, contrast, resize/reflow, target size, pointer alternatives, timing, error recovery, and language metadata should be treated as component invariants and end-to-end journey invariants.

Usability is related but distinct. ISO 9241-11 defines usability as effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction for specified users, goals, and context of use; ISO 9241-210 places human-centred activities throughout the life cycle. Thus a page can conform to WCAG while a person cannot efficiently complete a realistic task, cannot understand domain language, or experiences a fragile screen-reader workflow. Usability evidence is contextual and empirical: task success/accuracy, error recovery, time or interaction effort, confidence, perceived workload, and satisfaction should be collected with the assistive technology and environmental conditions actually used. A single heuristic review, a small convenience sample, or an automated conformance result cannot be treated as a population-wide usability estimate.

Evaluation methods are complementary. Static and automated checks are strong for deterministic properties such as missing required attributes, duplicate IDs, some name/role/value mappings, contrast calculations, target geometry, language metadata, and known ACT rules. They cannot reliably judge whether alternative text is meaningful, whether focus order preserves task meaning, whether a status message is noticed, whether a CAPTCHA or authentication flow imposes cognitive burden, whether a translation is culturally appropriate, or whether a user can recover from an error. Human expert inspection adds semantic and interaction reasoning; representative disabled users expose barriers and workarounds that experts may miss. The Mankoff-Fait-Tran comparison found complementary strengths among laboratory users, experts, automated tools, and remote testing; remote testing is not automatically equivalent to observed use.

Internationalization is a correctness and inclusion property. Internationalization (i18n) designs the product so localization (l10n) can adapt it to languages, scripts, regions, and cultures. Unicode provides code-point and bidirectional behavior, while CLDR/LDML and ECMA-402 provide locale identifiers, fallback, plural rules, collation, segmentation, number/currency/unit/date/time/time-zone formatting, and calendar data. Correctness must be tested at grapheme-cluster and rendered-layout boundaries, not only code-unit lengths. Bidirectional rendering requires logical-order data, explicit direction or isolation where needed, and tests with mixed Arabic/Hebrew, Latin, numbers, punctuation, URLs, form labels, and accessible names. Locale data is not a string substitution table: grammatical gender, plural categories, month context, numbering systems, calendars, first day of week, decimal/group separators, time zones, and culturally expected formats all affect behavior.

Compatibility is a matrix of browser engine/version, operating system, viewport and zoom, input modality, assistive technology/version, and locale/script—not a browser-name checkbox. WCAG's accessibility-support concept and WCAG-EM's baseline require teams to state which combinations are supported. Web Platform Tests and Interop 2026 provide valuable cross-browser signals for standardized platform behavior, including an accessibility-tree investigation, but passing platform tests does not prove application semantics or task usability. Evidence gaps remain: WCAG success criteria do not measure all disability experiences; published tool benchmarks predate current engines and AI-assisted tooling; assistive technology behavior changes by version and settings; human studies often use small, heterogeneous samples; and localization quality still requires language/culture expertise. These limitations argue for triangulated, versioned evidence and explicit uncertainty rather than a universal “accessible” label.
practical_architecture_and_implementatio:
Implement NFR-04 as a layered quality architecture with a traceable requirement-to-evidence chain.

1. Define a product accessibility contract. For each product surface, record WCAG 2.2 target (normally A/AA), applicable non-web/mobile interpretation, supported browsers and operating systems, assistive-technology baseline, input modalities, minimum viewport/zoom, supported locales/scripts/calendars, and essential user journeys. Use WCAG-EM's product-enclosure principle: include all views, states, routes, dialogs, overlays, third-party widgets, authenticated paths, error paths, and complete processes; do not infer site-wide conformance from a few attractive pages. Maintain a risk register for barriers affecting task completion, safety, privacy choices, or access to authentication.

2. Build accessible component contracts. Every control contract specifies semantic element or platform control, accessible name source, role/state/value mapping, keyboard and pointer behavior, focus entry/exit, focus visibility and overlay interaction, announcement/status behavior, error identification and recovery, minimum target geometry, text resizing/reflow behavior, language metadata, and RTL mirroring. Prefer native semantics; prohibit ARIA role overrides that conflict with host-language semantics; require synchronized DOM state and accessible-tree state. Include Storybook/component fixtures for empty, loading, validation-error, disabled, selected, expanded, long-label, translated, RTL, high-contrast, zoomed, and reduced-motion states.

3. Automate deterministic checks in every change pipeline. Run HTML/DOM and accessibility-tree checks after rendering, not only on source templates. Adopt ACT Rules Format 1.1-style rule records with rule ID/version, applicability, assumptions, accessibility-support baseline, expected outcomes (passed/failed/inapplicable/cantTell/untested), WCAG mapping, and examples. Use route/state coverage to exercise menus, dialogs, focus traps, live regions, authentication, client-side validation, pagination, drag alternatives, and permission/timeout branches. Automate contrast and non-text contrast, labels and names, language attributes, duplicate IDs, heading/landmark structure, keyboard reachability, focus visibility/obscuration, 24x24 CSS-pixel target checks, 320-CSS-pixel reflow, 200% text resize, text-spacing overrides, and color-independent status. Treat tool output as triage: a failure is actionable, a pass is bounded evidence, and cantTell/untested requires review.

4. Add manual expert and assistive-technology gates. For each critical journey, execute a keyboard-only pass (Tab/Shift+Tab, arrows, Enter/Space, Escape, no trap, logical order, restore focus), zoom/reflow and high-contrast/forced-colors pass, reduced-motion and touch/pointer pass, and screen-reader passes on at least one desktop and one mobile stack. Record actual browser, OS, AT, versions, settings, locale, viewport, zoom, input device, and expected versus observed accessible name/role/state/value and announcements. Use a representative baseline such as Chromium/Windows/NVDA, Chromium or Firefox/Windows/JAWS where business-critical, Safari/macOS/VoiceOver, and iOS/iPadOS VoiceOver plus Android/TalkBack; tailor the matrix to users and support commitments rather than treating this illustrative set as universal.

5. Run inclusive human-subject usability studies at decision points. Recruit people who actually use screen readers, magnification, keyboard/switch access, speech input, captions, alternative pointing, cognitive supports, and relevant languages; include people with intersecting and fluctuating disabilities. Co-design task scenarios with participants, pay fairly, provide accessible consent and materials, permit their own AT and settings, and avoid asking participants to simulate a disability. For formative studies, observe realistic task attempts and think-aloud/debriefing to find barriers and workarounds; for summative studies, preregister task definitions and metrics and report denominators, exclusions, learning effects, confidence intervals where appropriate, and qualitative severity. Separate accessibility defects, general usability friction, content/translation defects, and platform/AT defects so remediation ownership is clear.

6. Operate compatibility and internationalization as parameterized matrices. A representative matrix has rows for critical journeys/components and columns for browser engine/version, OS, device class/orientation, zoom/text size, input modality, AT, locale, script direction, calendar, and time zone. Prioritize pairwise combinations plus risk-based triples (for example, Arabic + RTL + VoiceOver + mobile Safari; German + long text + 400% zoom; Japanese IME + keyboard navigation; Hindi/Devanagari + screen reader; Hebrew + mixed numeric identifiers). Define outcomes as pass, pass with documented degradation, blocked, or not supported; require a rationale and user-impact assessment for exclusions. Use Interop/WPT for platform-level regressions, then app-level assertions for DOM/accessibility tree, focus, rendered geometry, and task completion. Test the oldest supported and current versions, not only latest.

7. Make i18n testable from the architecture. Store Unicode text and locale identifiers explicitly; normalize at system boundaries where product semantics require it; never slice visible text by code unit; test combining marks, surrogate pairs, emoji sequences, grapheme clusters, non-breaking spaces, zero-width joiners, and locale-specific case/ordering. Use BCP 47/Unicode locale tags and deterministic locale fallback. Format values with CLDR/ECMA-402 APIs rather than hand-built separators or date parsing; test Gregorian plus business-relevant non-Gregorian calendars, local digits, decimal/group separators, currencies, plural/select rules, units, time zones/DST, list and person-name conventions, and ambiguous dates. Test `dir`/CSS logical properties and bidi isolates with mixed-direction labels, numbers, punctuation, URLs, and accessible names. Add pseudolocalization with expansion and deliberately long words, but require native-speaker review for translation, grammar, cultural meaning, and terminology. Verify that localized accessible names, error messages, help, captions, and screen-reader pronunciation remain usable.

8. Preserve evidence and feedback. Store criterion-level findings in version control or an evidence store with product build, commit, route/state, sample rationale, test oracle/rule version, environment fingerprint, raw tool output, DOM and accessibility-tree snapshots, screenshots/video where useful, AT transcript, participant/task records, defect links, retest result, and known limitations. Generate machine-readable reports (EARL or an equivalent structured format) and human summaries. Trend open defects by severity and user impact, not a single aggregate score. Block release for critical journey blockers or regressions agreed in the contract; permit documented risk acceptance only with an owner, affected populations, workaround quality, expiry/retest date, and customer communication.

A practical CI cadence is: pre-commit/component checks for semantics and i18n-safe APIs; pull-request rendered checks and keyboard smoke tests; nightly route/state crawls over the support matrix; weekly or release-candidate manual AT review for changed critical journeys; and scheduled inclusive user studies and full WCAG-EM-style audits. Re-run after browser/OS/AT upgrades, design-system changes, locale-data upgrades, authentication changes, and third-party widget updates.

Representative compatibility/i18n matrix fields:
| Dimension | Required variation/evidence |
| Browser/platform | Chromium, Firefox, WebKit/Safari; oldest supported and current versions; desktop and mobile |
| Assistive technology | NVDA/JAWS/VoiceOver/TalkBack or user-relevant alternatives, with version/settings |
| Input/display | Keyboard, touch, switch/speech where relevant; portrait/landscape; 100%, 200%, 400% zoom; forced colors |
| Locale/script | en, a long-expansion locale, CJK/IME, Arabic or Hebrew RTL, Indic shaping, mixed-script identifiers |
| Formatting | decimal/group/currency, plural/list rules, time zone/DST, Gregorian and business-relevant alternate calendars |
| Evidence | environment fingerprint, rule IDs, screenshots/tree snapshots, transcript, task metrics, defect and retest links |

The architecture deliberately distinguishes normative conformance from empirical usability, platform compatibility, and localization quality. It also makes negative evidence visible: unknown, cantTell, unsupported, and blocked are first-class outcomes rather than silently converted to pass.

primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: Content must be robust enough that it can be interpreted by a wide variety of user agents, including assistive technologies.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: WCAG 2.2 is the normative web baseline and its Robust principle directly makes browser/AT interpretation part of the conformance problem. The current Recommendation page is the 12 December 2024 republished version; the original WCAG 2.2 Recommendation was published in 2023. Engineering should map criteria to rendered states and complete processes, include the new focus, dragging, target-size, redundant-entry, consistent-help, and accessible-authentication criteria, and report the selected A/AA/AAA level explicitly. WCAG's own scope caveat means a passing claim is not evidence that every disability experience or usability outcome is covered.

primary_evidence.source_title: ISO/IEC 40500:2025 — Information technology — W3C Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2
primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: International Organization for Standardization and International Electrotechnical Commission
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: WCAG 2.2 success criteria are written as testable statements that are not technology-specific.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: ISO/IEC 40500:2025 establishes WCAG 2.2 as an international standard while preserving technology-neutral, testable requirements. Teams should keep normative criterion outcomes separate from technology-specific techniques and record which technology, user-agent, and AT assumptions make a criterion accessibility-supported. The ISO page says this 2025 edition is published and under revision, so baselines should pin the edition and monitor successor status rather than silently mixing drafts with the standard.

primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: While most accessibility checks are not fully automatable, evaluation tools can significantly assist evaluators.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: The 23 July 2026 W3C Group Note supplies a defensible audit architecture: define scope and conformance target, define the accessibility-support baseline, explore product types and technologies, select structured plus random samples and complete processes, evaluate them, and report each outcome. It explicitly recommends involving people with disabilities and says the methodology does not replace quality assurance across development. Use it to prevent a scan of a few pages from becoming an unsupported site-wide claim.

primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: The test rules can be used for developing automated testing tools and manual testing methodologies.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: ACT Rules Format 1.1 (W3C Recommendation, 5 February 2026) gives automation and manual review a shared, versioned vocabulary. Its applicability, assumptions, accessibility-support context, examples, mappings, and explicit cantTell/untested outcomes are useful CI contract fields. ACT rules harmonize how a check is documented; they do not make subjective content judgments automatable and do not turn one implementation's rule set into complete WCAG coverage.

primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: W3C Accessible Rich Internet Applications Working Group
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: WAI-ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) is intended to be used as a supplement to native language semantics, not a replacement.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: ARIA 1.2 defines roles, states, properties, and their exposure through accessibility APIs. The normative direction to supplement rather than replace native semantics supports a design-system rule: use native controls first, then test custom widgets for accessible name, role, value, focus, keyboard behavior, state synchronization, and AT announcements across supported stacks. ARIA markup alone is not an interaction implementation and can create conflicts when it contradicts host-language semantics.

primary_evidence.source_title: Guidance on Applying WCAG 2.2 to Mobile Applications (WCAG2Mobile)
primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: W3C Mobile Accessibility Task Force and Accessibility Guidelines Working Group
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: This document provides informative guidance (guidance that is not normative and does not set requirements)
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: The 6 May 2025 Group Draft Note maps WCAG 2.2 A/AA criteria to native, mobile-web, and hybrid applications and treats a mobile screen as the comparable unit of conformance. It highlights orientation, reflow, touch alternatives, dragging, target size, redundant entry, and accessible authentication. Because the document is explicitly work in progress and non-normative, use it to design mobile scenarios and evidence, while citing WCAG/ISO for normative requirements.

primary_evidence.source_title: ISO 9241-210:2019 — Human-centred design for interactive systems
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: This document provides requirements and recommendations for human-centred design principles and activities throughout the life cycle of computer-based interactive systems.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: ISO 9241-210 makes human-centred design a life-cycle activity for web sites, applications, mobile phones, and other interactive systems. It is a process framework, not a prescribed usability test recipe; the ISO page states that detailed methods are outside scope. Translate it into accessibility-inclusive discovery, context-of-use models, participatory design, iterative evaluation, and release evidence rather than treating one late usability test as compliance.

primary_evidence.source_title: Common Industry Specification for Usability — Requirements (NISTIR 7432)
primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: Mary F. Theofanos, National Institute of Standards and Technology
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: The context of use: the intended users, their goals and tasks, associated equipment, and the physical and social environment
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: NISTIR 7432 operationalizes usability requirements as context of use, performance/satisfaction criteria, and test method/context. The same structure prevents accessibility studies from omitting the participant's own AT, device, environment, goals, or task constraints. It supports requirement-level acceptance criteria and reproducible reports, while its 2007 date means teams should adapt—not overstate—the historical guidance for modern mobile, remote, and assistive-technology contexts.

primary_evidence.source_title: Unicode Standard Annex #9 — Unicode Bidirectional Algorithm, Version 17.0.0
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: This annex describes the algorithm used to determine the directionality for bidirectional Unicode text.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: UAX #9 Version 17.0.0 (13 August 2025) is the normative algorithmic basis for rendering mixed-direction text. Test logical-order storage separately from visual order, and include isolates, embedding boundaries, paired punctuation, numbers, URLs, labels, and screen-reader accessible names. The annex notes that formatting characters affect display rather than parsing; applications therefore need explicit higher-level markup/CSS policy and regression tests to avoid bidi spillover and confusing or misleading output.

primary_evidence.source_title: Unicode Technical Standard #35 — Unicode Locale Data Markup Language (LDML), Version 48.2
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: This document describes an XML format (vocabulary) for the exchange of structured locale data.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: UTS #35 Version 48.2 (3 March 2026) provides the CLDR/LDML data model for locale identifiers, inheritance, numbers/currencies, dates/calendars, time zones, collation, plural rules, person names, keyboards, and message formatting. Use it to define locale fixtures and expected outputs rather than hard-coding English assumptions. Its stable, normative-reference status supports pinning CLDR data versions and testing changes as dependencies, including grammatical/contextual forms and alternate numbering systems.

primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: This Standard defines the application programming interface for ECMAScript objects that support programs that need to adapt to the linguistic
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: ECMA-402 13th Edition defines locale selection and inspection, collation/case conversion, pluralization, text segmentation, and number/date/time/duration/list formatting. It is an implementation contract for using locale-sensitive APIs instead of custom parsing and concatenation. Tests should assert both semantic values and rendered strings across supported locales, calendars, time zones, numbering systems, and plural categories, and should account for implementation/data-version differences.

primary_evidence.source_title: Interop 2026 — Web Platform Tests interoperability effort
primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: Web Platform Tests Interop Project (Apple, Bocoup, Google, Igalia, Microsoft, Mozilla, and community contributors)
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: The tests we selected will be continuously run on automated testing infrastructure.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: Interop 2026 uses WPT tests and continuously reports browser-engine pass rates. Its scope is standardized platform behavior, and the 2026 effort includes accessibility-tree consistency and mobile-testing investigations. It is strong evidence for browser compatibility regressions but not a substitute for application-level semantic, AT, locale, or task tests; teams should consume WPT signals and retain their own product assertions and support matrix.

primary_evidence.source_title: Is Your Web Page Accessible? A Comparative Study of Methods for Assessing Web Page Accessibility for the Blind
primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: Jennifer Mankoff, Holly Fait, and Tu Tran
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: All of the techniques, however, had different, complementary strengths and weaknesses.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: This ACM CHI study compared blind-user laboratory evaluation, expert review with and without screen readers, an automated tool, and remote blind-user testing. Its central result supports triangulation: no single method was sufficient, developers using a screen reader found about half of known problem classes, and remote testing had context-dependent weaknesses. The study is foundational but old; use its methodological lesson, not its historical tool rates, as a 2026 rule.

primary_evidence.source_title: Benchmarking Web Accessibility Evaluation Tools: Measuring the Harm of Sole Reliance on Automated Tests
primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: Markel Vigo, Justin Brown, and Vivienne Conway
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: Coverage is very narrow as, at most, 50% of the success criteria are covered.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: This ACM W4A benchmark measured six tools against WCAG 2.0 using coverage, completeness, and correctness and found substantial blind spots and false positives. The exact percentages should not be generalized to current scanners, WCAG 2.2, dynamic applications, or AI tooling; the reproducible principle remains that scanner passes cannot justify a conformance claim. Track per-rule false-positive/negative behavior and require manual and user evidence for subjective criteria.

primary_evidence.source_title: The Effects of ‘Not Knowing What You Don't Know’ on Web Accessibility for Blind Web Users
primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: Jeffrey P. Bigham, Irene Lin, and Saiph Savage
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: not knowing the source of a problem causes frustration and wastes time.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: The ACM ASSETS study with 30 sighted and 30 blind participants shows why technical accessibility and usability are intertwined: a blind user may not know whether content is missing, inaccessible, or merely hard to find. Human tests should capture uncertainty, recovery, time lost, and requests for sighted assistance—not just binary task completion—and design should expose clear structure, status, errors, and predictable navigation.

primary_evidence.source_title: Invisible, Unreadable, and Inaudible Cookie Notices: An Evaluation of Cookie Notices for Users with Visual Impairments
primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: James M. Clarke, Maryam Mehrnezhad, and Ehsan Toreini
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: the majority of cookie notices on these websites have some form of accessibility issues
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: This ACM Transactions on Accessible Computing study combined system analysis of 46 top UK websites with accessibility tools, text-only browsers, and screen readers, plus a 100-person user study. It demonstrates that real-world consent UI can fail contrast, headings, immediate announcement, and usable interaction even when it is visually prominent. Treat overlays and privacy-choice flows as critical complete processes, and test actual AT announcements and recovery rather than only DOM-level attributes.

failure_modes_and_antipatterns: Scanner-score gate: treating an automated percentage or a single tool's pass report as WCAG conformance. Automated checks cover only a subset, can miss dynamic states and meaningful content judgments, and can emit false positives; keep criterion-level manual and user evidence.

Source-only testing: inspecting templates or static DOM while missing post-render dialogs, live regions, focus changes, route transitions, validation errors, timeout/re-authentication branches, and third-party widgets.

ARIA as decoration: adding roles or labels to non-native elements without implementing keyboard behavior, focus management, state synchronization, accessible-name computation, or accessibility-API compatibility; conflicting ARIA/native semantics can be worse than native markup.

Keyboard theater: confirming that Tab reaches controls but not checking logical focus order, visible/non-obscured focus, Escape and dialog exit, restored focus, no traps, character-key shortcut conflicts, pointer alternatives, or completion of a complete process.

One-stack compatibility claim: testing only one browser, OS, viewport, or screen reader and generalizing to all users. AT output depends on browser engine, OS accessibility API, version, settings, input mode, and locale; pin a support baseline and test risk-based combinations.

Simulated disability substitution: asking sighted or non-disabled staff to use a screen-reader simulation, blindfold, or reduced-mobility exercise instead of involving people who use the relevant AT and have lived expertise. Simulation can supplement training but cannot establish usability.

Conformance-sample overclaim: evaluating a few representative pages and publishing a whole-site conformance claim despite untested states, templates, processes, authenticated areas, or external content. Document sample boundaries and use WCAG-EM enclosure/sampling rules.

Authentication barrier: password-only memory demands, inaccessible CAPTCHA, auto-clearing fields, disabled paste/password managers, short timeouts, or OTP/passkey flows that are not operable and announced with the user's AT. Test every authentication and recovery step against Accessible Authentication and realistic cognitive/motor needs.

Visual-only usability: accepting contrast and screenshot review while ignoring semantic structure, speech output, captions/transcripts, error announcements, reading order, input purpose, cognitive load, and the user's ability to understand system status.

Locale substitution: replacing strings without testing plural/gender/context, expansion, truncation, CJK/Indic shaping, IME input, locale fallback, number/currency/date/time-zone/calendar rules, person names, sorting, or localized accessible names and errors.

Bidi corruption: concatenating mixed-direction strings without explicit direction/isolation, slicing by code unit, or snapshotting only English/LTR layouts. This causes reordered punctuation/numbers, broken URLs/identifiers, incorrect reading order, and misleading labels.

Fixed-layout and zoom failure: hard-coded widths/heights, clipped focus rings, modal overlays covering focus, two-dimensional scrolling at 400% zoom, text-spacing loss, and target sizes below 24 by 24 CSS pixels. Test authored CSS overrides and mobile orientation, not only default screenshots.

Pseudolocalization overconfidence: assuming expansion and synthetic strings validate translation quality. Pseudolocalization finds layout/resource-key defects; native speakers and local users are needed for grammar, idiom, cultural appropriateness, pronunciation, and task meaning.

Evidence decay: retaining a one-time audit without environment fingerprints, rule versions, raw results, AT transcripts, locale data versions, retests, or browser/OS upgrade triggers. Compatibility and accessibility support change; evidence must be reproducible and re-baselined.

maturity_matrix.foundational: Adopt WCAG 2.2 A/AA criteria as traceable requirements; define an accessibility-support and browser/OS/AT baseline; use semantic native controls and an accessible component checklist; run deterministic automated checks plus keyboard, zoom/reflow, contrast, language, and basic screen-reader smoke tests on critical journeys; maintain a small locale set including long text and one RTL case; record criterion, environment, defect, and retest evidence. Do not publish an aggregate score as a conformance claim.
maturity_matrix.advanced: Apply WCAG-EM 2.0 enclosure and structured/random sampling to all views, states, complete processes, authenticated/error paths, and third-party content; implement ACT 1.1-style versioned rules with cantTell/untested outcomes; exercise rendered routes and state fixtures in CI; run a risk-based browser/OS/AT/mobile matrix and WPT/Interop regression checks; conduct formative studies with people using relevant AT and locales; measure task success, errors/recovery, effort/time, workload, and satisfaction; add pseudolocalization, Unicode/bidi, CLDR/ECMA-402, calendar/time-zone, IME, and 200/400% reflow suites.
maturity_matrix.expert_2026: Operate accessibility, usability, compatibility, and i18n as a release-quality system with product-specific contracts, design-system semantic invariants, accessibility-tree assertions, complete-process oracles, machine-readable EARL-equivalent evidence, and environment/locale dependency pinning. Use inclusive participatory research and recurring summative measurement with transparent uncertainty; stratify results by disability/AT/context and distinguish conformance, usability, platform, and localization defects. Continuously consume WPT/Interop and browser/AT changes, detect regressions across risk-based interaction/locale triples, and make blocked/unsupported/cantTell evidence visible. Release decisions use user-impact severity, critical-journey blockers, documented residual risk, owners, expiry/retest dates, and accessible customer communication rather than universal claims or vendor marketing scores.
